1:
Ellicott sets the chapter in its place, since the previous chapter had laid down the sin offering as it applies when the spiritual head, or the whole congregation, or the ruler, or a private member offends inadvertently, and the lawgiver now turns to the offering required when specific precepts have been violated. The first case is a failure to come forward as a witness after judicial adjuration has been uttered, and he would render it accordingly, because he heard the voice of adjuration and might be a witness. Henry explains the procedure that made such silence possible, that judges among the Jews could adjure not only the witness but the suspected person, contrary to the rule of English law that no man is bound to accuse himself, and he instances the high priest adjuring the Saviour, who had stood silent until then and thereupon answered. Clarke describes the same case as a man demanded by the civil magistrate to answer on oath who refuses to tell what he knows. Gill notices the wording, that soul is put for the person and is named particularly, on the authority of a Jewish commentator, because the soul possesses will and desire.

Calvin admits at once that the three offences named look very unlike one another, since concealing what one knows cannot arise from error, and he explains how he brings the first under that head all the same: he supposes a man induced by shame or fear to connive at an offence he is questioned about, so that without any design of perjuring himself he blinds himself and withholds what he would have said had he examined the matter duly. He then reports that commentators are not agreed on the sense of the key word. Wesley takes it the other way and identifies the thing heard as cursing or blasphemy or execration, whether against a neighbour or against God, arguing that the crime must be of so high a nature that a hearer was bound to reveal it and prosecute the guilty. He also glosses the closing phrase as meaning not the iniquity but the punishment of it, a use he finds elsewhere in the Pentateuch. Keil and Delitzsch take the second case at its widest, any defilement whatever to which a man is exposed, whether from the carcase of an unclean beast or from the uncleanness of a man.

On the rash oath the readings differ in what they think the guilt consists of. Ellicott renders the phrase as speaking heedlessly with the lips, an oath uttered in thoughtlessness or passion without the heart realising it, and takes the pair to do evil or to do good as an idiom embracing all human action whatever, as elsewhere in the Pentateuch. Clarke thinks rash promises are meant and states the dilemma plainly: if a man vows to do an evil act it would be criminal to keep the oath, yet he is guilty for having made it, and if he neglects the good he vowed he is guilty too, so that either way he must confess and bring his offering. Calvin locates the fault not in the breaking but in the carelessness, since sound religion would have renewed the recollection of the vow, and where no anxiety to fulfil it appears there was no serious desire to do so; he adds why the commandment was needed, that men who had pledged their faith and broken it in thoughtlessness might otherwise think themselves released. Wesley notes the oath may bind a man against himself or his neighbour.
5:
The confession is treated by all of them as more than a formality. Clarke states its necessity in the strongest terms, that restitution alone was not sufficient, since a man might make restitution without being much humbled, whereas confession of sin has a direct tendency to humble the soul, which is why the Scriptures require it so frequently; without humiliation, he says, there can be no salvation. Wesley locates it, that the confession was to be made before the Lord in the place of public worship, and extends its reach beyond this case: by parity of reason and by comparison of other passages it belonged to the other sacrifices for sin as well, being a constant companion of them. Ellicott simply refers the reader to the form of words used in the second Temple. Gill reports the Jewish enumeration of the offences here summed up, in one of the four things, which a rabbinic authority lists as the oath of witness, the pollution of the sanctuary, the pollution of its holy things, and a vain oath. Keil and Delitzsch note that the three cases are gathered under a single expression for the purpose of introducing what follows.

Ellicott makes two observations about the sacrifice named. The word is properly trespass offering and is so rendered in thirty-five of the thirty-six places where it stands for a sacrifice; and in this section, unlike the sin offering of the previous chapter, no distinction is drawn between ranks of offender, so that there is no special legislation for the high priest, the congregation or the prince, and the spiritual officer and temporal sovereign stand on a level with the ordinary layman. He would also render the victim as a sheep or a shaggy she-goat. Calvin sees a different principle beginning here, the distinction between rich and poor, which he thinks applies backwards as well and shows that the order of the chapter is not exactly kept, since the inserted cases interrupt the thread. What matters to him is that the poor are not pressed beyond their means, the grades of offering being appointed so that a man who could not manage two pigeons might be quit for a small measure of flour; from which he infers that God's design was only to show the one true means of atonement.

Wesley raises a difficulty the others pass over and answers it. If a man who touched an unclean thing was cleansed by simple washing elsewhere in the law, why should confession and a sacrifice be required of him here? His solution is that this passage means one who, being so unclean, then came into the tabernacle; a man who did that knowing himself unclean was to be cut off, while a man who did it in ignorance, which is the case supposed here, was on discovering it to bring this offering. Gill reads the offering typically, as figuring the sacrifice of Christ, whose soul was made an offering for sin, and notes that the Hebrew word used there for a trespass offering is the same word that stands in this verse. Keil and Delitzsch describe the ritual for the poor man's birds with some precision, the head pinched off from opposite the neck, in the nape just below the head, without entirely severing it; — a level of detail the chapter nowhere else descends to.
7:
Henry reads the graduated offering as the most generous provision in the law: the cost of the sin offering was brought lower than that of any other offering, so that no man's poverty should ever bar his pardon, and the poorest of all might have atonement made for them if it be not their own fault — thus the poor are evangelized, and no man shall be able to say he had not wherewithal. Ellicott states the exception more narrowly, that poverty was the only ground on which the substitution was allowed, and explains why doves were chosen, being plentiful and cheap in Palestine. He also answers a technical question the substitution raises: since the fat parts of a bird cannot be separated for the altar, and burning the whole would turn a trespass offering into a whole burnt offering, two doves were required so that one might serve for each purpose. Wesley notes the order in which they were offered, the sin offering first because it was for that particular sin and the burnt offering after because it was for sins in general, and draws the lesson that we are not to rest in general confessions.

On the lowest grade the commentators reach for a measure and do not agree. Clarke reckons the tenth of an ephah at about three quarts, the whole ephah containing a little more than seven gallons and a half; Ellicott makes it a little less than half a gallon, and Wesley about six pints. Gill takes the case as supposing a man in the poorest circumstances he can well be, and finds in the provision the grace of God, that atonement and forgiveness are provided for the poorest as well as for the rich. On the withholding of oil and frankincense Ellicott gives the technical reason, that the offering must be kept distinct from the meal offering or its character as a sin offering would be destroyed. Wesley offers the same reason and then two others: that the abstaining from pleasant things was a fit expression of sorrow for sin, and that it signified how by his sins the offerer deserved to be deprived both of the oil of gladness, which is the gifts and comforts of the Spirit, and of that gracious acceptance of prayer which incense stands for.

Ellicott corrects the closing verse on a small point with a practical consequence. The word remnant is not in the original and is better left out, since apart from the handful taken to burn on the altar the whole tenth part of the ephah belonged to the priest; and he adds a distinction from later practice, that this held only when the offerer was a layman, since when a priest committed the offence and brought this offering the whole tenth was burnt on the altar as with the meal offering. Keil and Delitzsch describe the same lowest grade from the other side, that a man who could not afford even two pigeons was to bring the tenth of an ephah of fine flour with neither oil nor frankincense upon it, because it is a sin offering. Gill reads the burning of the handful as an emblem of the painful sufferings by which atonement was made. Ellicott notes that the sin spoken of at the close is one of the three named at the head of the chapter, so that the whole graduated provision belongs to those cases and not to some new class of offence.
14:
Ellicott notes the fresh introduction, since the formula implies another communication made at a different time and setting out a further development of the law. Henry marks the same division of subject, that the preceding verses concerned offerings which went by both names, sin offering and trespass offering, while here begin those that are properly and peculiarly trespass offerings, made to atone for wrongs done to a neighbour; and he divides such wrongs into those in holy things, which the present verses cover, and those in common things, which the next chapter takes up. He explains why the holy things make a distinct case, since a man who alienated them or converted them to his own use trespassed against the priests, to whose care they were entrusted and whose benefit they were. Calvin argues the same point from the victim rather than the subject: God now requires a male where before an ewe lamb or female kid sufficed, and since a ram is more valuable it follows that a heavier offence is being punished, the heinousness depending on the quality of the act when a man has wronged not a mortal but God himself.

What counts as a trespass in holy things is answered by example rather than definition. Clarke takes the law to concern sacrilege and fraud in spiritual matters, instancing the neglect to consecrate or redeem the firstborn, the withholding of firstfruits and tithes, and, on rabbinic authority, the making of secular gain out of divine things, the keeping back of part of the price of what was dedicated, or the withholding of what a man had vowed. Ellicott gives much the same list and adds a lexical point, that the word here rendered trespass is not the one so rendered a few verses later but a word meaning literally to cover and so to act covertly or faithlessly, used especially of a sacred covenant broken with God or between husband and wife. Gill instances the payment of tithes and firstfruits and the eating of sacred things. Calvin includes both vows voluntarily made and the offering of a defective victim, anything by which God is defrauded of his right in an oblation. Wesley adds the boundary that makes the offering possible at all, since a man who did the thing knowingly was to be cut off.

The estimation and the added fifth are worked out concretely. Clarke explains that the defraud was to be valued at the number of shekels it was worth or would sell for, paid down with a fifth part more, and a ram brought besides, admitting that there is an obscurity in the text but taking this to be its meaning. Wesley reads the estimation as made by the priest, and at this moment by Moses, who was still performing the priest's part, and calls the payment an additional charge and punishment over and above the ram. Gill thinks the verse about making amends favours understanding the estimation of the damage done rather than of the ram. Ellicott sets out the arithmetic as it was reckoned in the time of Christ, where the principal counted as four-fifths of the whole and the missing fifth was added, so that a man who had consumed holy things worth four shekels paid five — which is by our reckoning a quarter rather than a fifth. He notes besides that no distinction is drawn here between the high priest, a prince and a private man.
17:
Ellicott explains what makes this last case distinct, that a trespass offering is required where a man only suspects he has put sacred property to his own use and can no longer remember which holy thing it was. In the exposition current during the second Temple this was accordingly called the Doubtful Offering, in contrast with the Certain Offering enacted just above, and he gives an example of the doubt, a man uncertain whether his fault lay in not delivering the firstfruits or in having used some other sacred property. Calvin considers whether the expressions here are general, briefly confirming what has gone before, or restricted to particular cases, and comes down for the second while allowing that a repetition would be no absurdity, since it would cut off every subterfuge from the disobedient. Wesley distinguishes the two laws by their subject rather than by the offender's certainty, the former concerning the alienation of holy things from sacred to common use and this one other miscarriages about holy things and holy duties, which he gathers from the way the closing verse names it a trespass against the Lord in a proper and peculiar sense.

Ellicott would improve two renderings in the middle verse. The estimation is the valuation of Moses, by which the ram is to be worth two shekels; and the clause about not knowing should read though he wist not, meaning that he does not know the precise sacred thing he used, exactly as the same phrase is rendered a verse earlier. From this he draws the one substantial difference between the doubtful case and the certain one: because the case is doubtful the offender is exempt from the additional fifth part which a man had to pay who indisputably committed the offence in ignorance. Gill notes only that the same victim is required as before. Calvin reads the requirement of a ram without blemish and of full value as showing once more how those must purge themselves who have been too stingy in their oblations, and takes the reason added at the close to apply to every mode of expiation in the chapter: a man who pretends ignorance, having sinned inconsiderately or contracted defilement through forgetfulness, is still guilty before God until he makes reconciliation, and ignorance offered as a cover for a fault does not absolve.

Gill states the principle the closing verse rests on, that no sin of any kind may be overlooked or passed by or forgiven without a sacrifice, and reports a rabbinic inference from the wording, that where an offering is said to be to the Lord it was not lawful for the priests to eat of it. Ellicott makes the same point about the name, that although the prescribed fifth is here dispensed with the offering is still a trespass offering, because the man's conscience tells him he has trespassed. Clarke turns from the case to the reader and does not spare him. Considering the purity of God and the breadth of his commandment against our slowness to believe and our cold performance of sacred duties, it is no wonder that sinfulness is found in our holy things; but he judges a second evil worse than the first, the endeavour of religious people to reconcile themselves to that state and defend it as both unavoidable and useful, useful because they suppose it keeps them humble — whereas, he answers, the more inward sin a man has the more pride he will feel, and the less, the more humility.
